citations.quote:
Let $Q$ be any finite acyclic quiver over $\mathbb F_q$, including wild
quivers, and let $Z_-$ and $Z_+$ be any two assignments of upper-half-plane
charges $z_i\in\mathbb H$. In the dimension completion of the subobject-first
Hall algebra,
$$A_{\mathrm{all}}=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z\ \mathrm{decreasing}}S_Z(\phi),\qquad \Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):0\ne\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}\}.$$
The product is degreewise finite and includes all semistable objects, whether
stable or strictly semistable. Applying either Euler integration $I$ or skew
integration $J$ gives equal completed ordered products for $Z_-$ and $Z_+$.
Each integrated ordered product has constant term $1$ and is a unit in its
completed quantum torus; conjugation by the two equal products therefore gives
the same continuous automorphism.
No generic-stability, finite-type, 3-Calabi–Yau, orientation-data, or analytic
convergence assumption is used.

Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, where $Q_0,Q_1$ are finite
sets and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ are the source and target maps. Let $k=\mathbb F_q$
with $q>1$, and assign to each vertex $i\in Q_0$ a charge
$z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$. A
finite-dimensional representation $M$ assigns a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $M_i$ to each vertex and a linear map
$M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each arrow; its dimension vector is
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_k M_i)_{i\in Q_0}$. Put
$Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ and, for nonzero
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, put
$\phi_Z(\mathbf d)=\arg Z(\mathbf d)/\pi$ using the principal argument. For
$M\ne0$, set $\phi_Z(M)=\phi_Z(\mathbf d(M))$. Call $M$
$Z$-semistable when every nonzero subrepresentation has phase at most
$\phi_Z(M)$. Include the zero representation as semistable with no assigned
phase.

Use the small finitary abelian skeleton of these representations. Its Hall
algebra has basis $\delta_M$ indexed by isomorphism classes, and the
subobject-first convention is
$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L}f(U)g(L/U)$, with distinct embedded
subobjects counted separately. Its dimension completion is the product of
the finite-dimensional homogeneous components. For integer dimension
vectors define the bilinear Euler form and its skew-symmetrization by
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,\qquad \langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d).$$

For a phase $\phi$, let
$$S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\ne[0]\\M\ Z\text{-semistable}\\\phi_Z(M)=\phi}}\delta_M,$$
where $\delta_M$ is the characteristic function of the isomorphism class
$[M]$ and $\delta_0$ is the Hall unit. The Euler and skew integrations are
the continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad t=\sqrt q>0,$$
as proved for this finite-field category by the Euler and skew integration
theorem. Their completed targets have bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$ and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$

Write $\Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0},\
\mathbf e\ne0\}$ and order its elements decreasingly. Define the Euler and
skew Hall spectrum generators by
$$P_Z^{E}:=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow} I(S_Z(\phi)),\qquad P_Z^{\mathrm{sk}}:=\mathop{*}_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow}J(S_Z(\phi)).$$
In each product the largest phase is the leftmost factor and multiplication
is in the corresponding completed torus. In any fixed total-dimension degree
$D$, only dimension vectors with $\sum_i d_i\le D$ and their finitely many
phases can contribute. Thus these are degreewise formal products in the
specified completion; no analytic convergence is asserted.

These generators describe the Euler or skew integration of finite-field
semistable representation groupoids. Calling such data protected BPS indices,
dimensions of physical state spaces, or spectra of a four-dimensional
supersymmetric model is an additional dictionary, not part of this
mathematical definition.

derivations.claim:
For each of $Z_-$ and $Z_+$ the hypotheses of [F1] hold. The
decreasing-phase Hall factors in [F1] are the $S_Z(\phi)$ of [F2], and its
continuous integrations are the maps used in [F2]. Therefore the two
Euler-integrated products are equal and the two skew-integrated products are
equal in their respective completions. By [F2] these are exactly
$P_{Z_-}^E=P_{Z_+}^E$ and
$P_{Z_-}^{\mathrm{sk}}=P_{Z_+}^{\mathrm{sk}}$.

Let $P$ be either generator and write $P=1+G$. Every term of $G$ has
positive total dimension, so for each total-dimension bound $D$ only the
finitely many powers $G^n$ with $n\le D$ contribute to
$\sum_{n\ge0}(-G)^n$ in degrees at most $D$. The finite geometric identity
in each such truncation gives both $P\sum_{n\ge0}(-G)^n=1$ and
$\sum_{n\ge0}(-G)^nP=1$ degree by degree. Hence $P$ is a unit. Multiplication
is continuous in the stated completion, so $a\mapsto PaP^{-1}$ is a
continuous automorphism with inverse $a\mapsto P^{-1}aP$. The equal
generators from step 1.1 therefore induce equal automorphisms.

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over a finite quiver and charge assignments; it makes no empty-set or empty-domain claim beyond the degree-zero unit handled below.

boundaries.evidence: The zero representation contributes the degree-zero unit 1 to each S_Z(phi), as stated in the Definition and in F1.
For a one-vertex quiver there is only one nonzero phase in each chamber, so the completed factorization is the all-object sum in the Statement.
Equal-phase and strictly semistable factors remain included in the HN product in the Statement and F1.
Every vertex charge lies in the open upper half-plane, so every nonzero dimension vector has phase in (0,1), as stated in the Definition and F1.

boundaries.reason: The finite-field Hall and HN arguments use only finite-dimensional spaces and finite sets; no choice axiom is used.
The proposition is an equality of generators and induced automorphisms, not a biconditional.
The proposition is an equality of generators and induced automorphisms, not a biconditional.

finite_checks.case: one-vertex quiver through total dimension two
finite_checks.calculation: For Q with one vertex and no arrows, every vector-space representation is semistable at the unique vertex phase. Changing the positive upper-half-plane charge changes no phase ordering or factor. Thus both chamber products are the same single all-object factor in every checked degree.
finite_checks.disposition: Direct boundary calculation from the definition; it checks the degenerate one-phase case and does not substitute for the general supplier theorem.

citations.quote:
Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite quiver: $Q_0$ and $Q_1$ are finite sets,
and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ give the source and target of each arrow. Assume $Q$ has
no directed cycles. For a field $K$, a finite-dimensional representation $M$
assigns a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $M_i$ to each $i\in Q_0$ and a
linear map $M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each $a\in Q_1$. A morphism is a
family of linear maps at the vertices commuting with all arrow maps. Write
$\mathcal A_Q(K)$ for this category and
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_K M_i)_{i\in Q_0}\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$ for its dimension
vector. For the finite-field Hall branch, fix $k=\mathbb F_q$ and write
$\mathcal A_Q=\mathcal A_Q(k)$. The next lemma proves the abelian and Euler
properties over any field; over $k$ it constructs a small finitary abelian
skeleton of $\mathcal A_Q$, so $\mathcal A_Q$ is essentially small.

For $\mathbf d,\mathbf e\in\mathbb Z^{Q_0}$ define the bilinear form
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,$$
and its skew-symmetrization
$\langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)$.
The next lemma proves that $\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(N))$ is the
Hom-minus-Yoneda-Ext$^1$ dimension for this arrow convention.

Fix $z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ for each
vertex and extend $Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ additively. If
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$ is nonzero, then
$\operatorname{Im}Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i\operatorname{Im}z_i>0$; thus its
principal argument lies in $(0,\pi)$. For a nonzero representation $M$, put
$\phi_Z(M)=\arg Z(\mathbf d(M))/\pi\in(0,1)$. Call
$M$ **$Z$-semistable** if every nonzero subrepresentation $U\subseteq M$
satisfies $\phi_Z(U)\le\phi_Z(M)$, and **$Z$-stable** if the inequality is
strict for every proper nonzero subrepresentation.

For the semistable groupoids and stacks below, include the zero representation
as semistable without assigning it a phase. Stable objects and HN factors
remain nonzero.

For a dimension vector $\mathbf d$, let
$$\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf d}(Q)=\prod_{a:i\to j} \operatorname{Hom}_k(k^{d_i},k^{d_j}),\qquad G_{\mathbf d}=\prod_{i\in Q_0}\operatorname{GL}_{d_i,k}.$$
The group $G_{\mathbf d}$ acts by change of bases. Define
$\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)$ geometrically: its points over an
algebraic closure $\bar k$ are representations for which every nonzero
$\bar k$-subrepresentation satisfies the semistability inequality. The
associated quotient stack is
$\mathfrak M^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)=[\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)/G_{\mathbf d}]$.
For $\mathbf d=0$, set $\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf0}=\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf0}=\operatorname{Spec}k$.
The group $G_{\mathbf0}$ is trivial, so its rational-point groupoid has one
zero object, trivial automorphism group, and cardinality $1$.
Here $[X/G]$ denotes the groupoid-valued quotient: over a scheme $S$ its
objects are $G$-torsors on $S$ with equivariant maps to $X$, and its arrows
are equivariant isomorphisms over $S$. The openness lemma below proves that
$\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}$ is open.

For a finite groupoid $\mathcal G$, define its groupoid cardinality by
$$|\mathcal G|=\sum_{[x]\in\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal G)} \frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal G}(x)|}.$$
The rational-point groupoid of $\mathfrak M^{ss}_{\mathbf d}$ is finite, and
the finite-field descent lemma identifies it with the groupoid of finite-field
semistable representations and their isomorphisms. No Calabi–Yau structure,
potential, orientation data, vanishing cycles, or physical state-counting
identification is part of this definition.

Fix $Q$, $k=\mathbb F_q$, and $Z$ as in
[[def-finite-acyclic-quiver-stability-data]]. For a representation $M$, write
$a_M=|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal A_Q}(M)|$ and let $\delta_M$ be the basis
function of its isomorphism class. Let $\mathcal S_Q$ be the small finitary
abelian skeleton constructed in
[[lem-finite-acyclic-quiver-representations-are-finitary-hereditary-with-euler-form]].
Define $H_Q:=H_{\mathcal S_Q,\mathbb Q}$, identifying its basis with the
isomorphism classes of $\mathcal A_Q$. Fullness and transport of subobjects
and cokernels along isomorphisms preserve the Hall coefficients. Thus $H_Q$ is
the direct sum over those classes, with rational
coefficients and the quotient-first untwisted Hall product of
[[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]]. In that convention $[A]*_{qf}[B]$ counts
sequences $0\to B\to L\to A\to0$, and identify the basis symbol $[M]$ with
the characteristic function $\delta_M$. Define the **subobject-first** product
by $f\star g:=g*_{qf}f$. Then
$$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L} f(U)g(L/U),$$
where the sum is over subobject classes of $L$: monomorphisms into $L$ modulo
isomorphisms of their domains commuting with the monomorphism. Distinct
embedded subobjects are counted separately even when their domains are
isomorphic. Put
$\kappa_M=a_M\delta_M$.

For $\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, let $H_{Q,\mathbf d}$ be the span of
classes of dimension vector $\mathbf d$. It is finite-dimensional: the
representation set on the standard spaces $k^{d_i}$ is finite. Define the
dimension completion
$$\widehat H_Q=\prod_{\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}}H_{Q,\mathbf d}.$$
The product is extended degreewise; each coefficient uses finitely many
decompositions $\mathbf d=\mathbf a+\mathbf b$. There is no analytic
convergence assertion. The all-object and phase factors are
$$A_{\mathrm{all}}=\sum_{[M]}\delta_M,\qquad S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\\M\ne0,\ \phi_Z(M)=\phi,\ M\ Z\text{-semistable}}}\delta_M.$$
Each is an element of $\widehat H_Q$ because each homogeneous component has
finite support.

Let $t=\sqrt q>0$ and $K_q=\mathbb Q(\sqrt q)$. Take the completed Euler
torus and skew torus over $K_q$, with bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$, respectively, and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$
Their completions use the same dimension product. The next theorem proves
associativity and gives the continuous Euler and skew integration maps.

Let $\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and define
$\phi(z)=\arg(z)/\pi\in(0,1)$. For $z,w\in\mathbb H$, the phase of $z+w$
lies between $\phi(z)$ and $\phi(w)$, strictly between them when they are
unequal and equal to their common value when they coincide.

Let $Q$ be finite and acyclic, let $k=\mathbb F_q$, and give every vertex an
arbitrary charge $z_i\in\mathbb H$. Over any field extension $K/k$, every
finite-dimensional representation has a unique filtration
$$0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$$
whose nonzero factors $M_j/M_{j-1}$ are $Z$-semistable and have strictly
decreasing phases. If $M$ is defined over $k$, the unique filtration of its
scalar extension $M_{\bar k}=M\otimes_k\bar k$ is Frobenius invariant and
descends to $k$. Consequently geometric
semistability of an $\mathbb F_q$-representation is equivalent to
semistability tested only on its $\mathbb F_q$-subrepresentations. Write
$|\mathbf d|=\sum_i d_i$ for total dimension.

Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver over $k=\mathbb F_q$, let
$t=\sqrt q>0$, and use the subobject-first completion and tori from
[[def-subobject-first-completed-finite-quiver-hall-algebra-and-tori]]. The
degree-completed Hall product is associative and unital. The continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))} \frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)}$$
are unital algebra homomorphisms to the completed tori with products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}, \qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$
These are separate normalizations: the first is the Euler form target, while
the second uses the skew-symmetrized form and the diagonal factor
$t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf d)}$.

Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, where $Q_0,Q_1$ are finite
sets and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ are the source and target maps. Let $k=\mathbb F_q$
with $q>1$, and assign to each vertex $i\in Q_0$ a charge
$z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$. A
finite-dimensional representation $M$ assigns a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $M_i$ to each vertex and a linear map
$M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each arrow; its dimension vector is
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_k M_i)_{i\in Q_0}$. Put
$Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ and, for nonzero
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, put
$\phi_Z(\mathbf d)=\arg Z(\mathbf d)/\pi$ using the principal argument. For
$M\ne0$, set $\phi_Z(M)=\phi_Z(\mathbf d(M))$. Call $M$
$Z$-semistable when every nonzero subrepresentation has phase at most
$\phi_Z(M)$. Include the zero representation as semistable with no assigned
phase.

Use the small finitary abelian skeleton of these representations. Its Hall
algebra has basis $\delta_M$ indexed by isomorphism classes, and the
subobject-first convention is
$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L}f(U)g(L/U)$, with distinct embedded
subobjects counted separately. Its dimension completion is the product of
the finite-dimensional homogeneous components. For integer dimension
vectors define the bilinear Euler form and its skew-symmetrization by
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,\qquad \langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d).$$

For a phase $\phi$, let
$$S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\ne[0]\\M\ Z\text{-semistable}\\\phi_Z(M)=\phi}}\delta_M,$$
where $\delta_M$ is the characteristic function of the isomorphism class
$[M]$ and $\delta_0$ is the Hall unit. The Euler and skew integrations are
the continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad t=\sqrt q>0,$$
as proved for this finite-field category by the Euler and skew integration
theorem. Their completed targets have bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$ and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$

Write $\Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0},\
\mathbf e\ne0\}$ and order its elements decreasingly. Define the Euler and
skew Hall spectrum generators by
$$P_Z^{E}:=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow} I(S_Z(\phi)),\qquad P_Z^{\mathrm{sk}}:=\mathop{*}_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow}J(S_Z(\phi)).$$
In each product the largest phase is the leftmost factor and multiplication
is in the corresponding completed torus. In any fixed total-dimension degree
$D$, only dimension vectors with $\sum_i d_i\le D$ and their finitely many
phases can contribute. Thus these are degreewise formal products in the
specified completion; no analytic convergence is asserted.

These generators describe the Euler or skew integration of finite-field
semistable representation groupoids. Calling such data protected BPS indices,
dimensions of physical state spaces, or spectra of a four-dimensional
supersymmetric model is an additional dictionary, not part of this
mathematical definition.

Let $Q$ be any finite acyclic quiver over $k=\mathbb F_q$, with no
finite-representation-type restriction, and let $Z_-$ and $Z_+$ assign a charge in
$\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ to every vertex. Use the
subobject-first dimension completion and the Euler and skew integrations
defined on this A page. Then
$$P_{Z_-}^E=P_{Z_+}^E,\qquad P_{Z_-}^{\mathrm{sk}}=P_{Z_+}^{\mathrm{sk}}.$$
Each is a unit with constant term $1$ in its own completed quantum torus.
Consequently conjugation by the two generators defines the same continuous
automorphism on each corresponding completed torus. The products and
automorphisms are formal in the dimension completion. This is a finite-field
Hall identity only; it makes no physical state-counting identification.

derivations.claim:
After choosing bases at both vertices, a representation of dimension
$(1,1)$ is the scalar arrow $a\in k$. A change of bases
$(g_1,g_2)\in k^\times\times k^\times$ sends it to $g_2ag_1^{-1}$.
Therefore zero remains zero and every nonzero $a$ is isomorphic to $1$.
For $M_0$, every pair $(g_1,g_2)$ is an automorphism, so
$|\operatorname{Aut}(M_0)|=(q-1)^2$. For $M_1$, the automorphism condition
is $g_2=g_1$, so $|\operatorname{Aut}(M_1)|=q-1$.

A proper nonzero subrepresentation of a $(1,1)$ representation can
only have dimension $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$. The latter is always preserved by
the arrow, whereas the former is preserved exactly when $a=0$. Hence the
subobject-first product counts one $S_1$ subobject in $M_0$ and none in
$M_1$, while it counts one $S_2$ subobject in each. The corresponding
quotients are $S_2$ for the first count and $S_1$ for the second; this gives
the two displayed Hall products.

Each $S_i$ is stable because it has no proper nonzero subobject. The
phase of $M_a$ is the phase of $z_1+z_2$, strictly between the two simple
phases by [F3] when they differ. If
$\phi_Z(S_1)>\phi_Z(S_2)$, the only proper nonzero subobject $S_2$ of $M_1$
has lower phase, so $M_1$ is stable; $M_0$ has both simples as
subobjects and its unique HN factors are $S_1,S_2$. If
$\phi_Z(S_2)>\phi_Z(S_1)$, $S_2$ destabilizes $M_1$ and
$0\subset S_2\subset M_1$ has factors $S_2,S_1$; the split object $M_0$
has the same ordered factors. If the phases are equal, all proper
nonzero subobjects of both objects have the same phase as the object, so
both objects are semistable in the same phase factor. The uniqueness in
[F4] shows that these are exactly their HN placements.

For either unequal-phase chamber, the Hall product has coefficient one
on each of $M_0,M_1$ in degree $\mathbf d$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1; on the
wall both occur in one semistable factor. Since
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=
\chi_Q(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2)=1$,
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)=0$, and
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=-1$, [F5] and step 1.1 give
$$I(\delta_{M_0}+\delta_{M_1})=\left(\frac1{(q-1)^2}+\frac1{q-1}\right)X^{\mathbf d}=\frac q{(q-1)^2}X^{\mathbf d},$$
while the reversed product of simple factors has the same coefficient
because $X^{\mathbf e_2}X^{\mathbf e_1}
=qX^{\mathbf d}$. For the skew integration,
$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf d)=1$ and
$\langle\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\rangle=-1$; hence
$$J(\delta_{M_0}+\delta_{M_1})=\left(\frac t{(q-1)^2}+\frac t{q-1}\right)x^{\mathbf d}=\frac{t^3}{(q-1)^2}x^{\mathbf d},$$
and the reversed simple-factor product has coefficient
$t^2t/(q-1)^2=t^3/(q-1)^2$ as well, using $q=t^2$. This proves the
stated finite-degree comparison and its wall case without assigning a
physical interpretation.

boundaries.reason: The example fixes the nonempty one-arrow quiver and dimension vector (1,1); it does not claim a formula for an empty quiver.

boundaries.evidence: The zero arrow M_0 and its two proper nonzero subobjects are counted in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
The one nonzero-arrow orbit M_1, its diagonal automorphisms, and its unique S_2 subobject are counted in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
The equal-phase wall is checked explicitly in step 3.1; both classes are semistable in one phase factor.
The charges lie in the open upper half-plane and the phase-sum lemma keeps all nonzero phases inside (0,1), as stated in the Example.

The example gives explicit counts and phase cases, not a biconditional.

finite_checks.calculation: The two arrow scalars are 0 and 1, and both automorphism groups have order 1. For phi_1>phi_2 the Euler coefficient is 1+1=2 and the skew coefficient is t+t=2t. For phi_2>phi_1 the simple-factor Euler twist is q=2 and the skew twist is t=sqrt(2), giving 2 and t^3=2t.
finite_checks.disposition: Direct enumeration of all arrow maps over F_2 and substitution into the proved general formulas.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked Verification 1.1--4.1 and all seven cited item suppliers against their current Definitions/Statements, reading the phase lemma, HN lemma, integration theorem and Hall wall-crossing proofs. The k^times x k^times action has exactly the zero and nonzero arrow orbits, with stabilizer orders (q-1)^2 and q-1. The only possible proper nonzero subspaces have dimensions (1,0) and (0,1); the former is invariant iff a=0 and the latter always is. Thus embedded-subobject Hall coefficients are one, not automorphism-weighted counts. With upper-half-plane charges, the strict between-phase lemma proves M1 stable iff phi1>phi2, both descending HN cases, and semistability of both objects on the wall. I-weights sum to q/(q-1)^2; chi(d,d)=1 gives J-weights t*q/(q-1)^2=t^3/(q-1)^2. Checked opposite Euler/skew arguments and simple-factor products including the stable M1 contribution. At q=2 both stabilizer orders are 1 and the coefficients become 2 and 2*sqrt(2). Zero object is the phase-factor unit; equal-phase wall, all q>1, finite basis choices and no AC, and degreewise formal completion are accounted for. TikZ arrow 1:k to 2:k labelled a matches the algebraic maps; proof is diagram-independent. Bridgeland 1611.03696 §§3.4,4.5--4.6 supplies the scope and HN/A2 comparison; Reineke math/0204059 Proposition 2.5 and §4 uses a twisted slope convention; Schiffmann math/0611617 §1.3 uses a quotient-first twist. His Example 3.15 has an Ext-direction inconsistency, so it is contextual only and the actual directions are verified algebraically here. No physical or empirical state-counting claim is inferred. No repair needed.
